concept: Design system governance and component lifecycle
summary: Source-anchored research for Design system governance and component lifecycle. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: GOV.UK’s contribution criteria make inclusive evidence part of publication readiness: components must work in research with a representative sample including users with disabilities, and across browsers, assistive technologies and devices. The criteria also require clarity about the contexts actually tested. (low confidence)

Preply’s practitioner account distinguishes coverage (usage) from adoption (correct usage). It also tracks documentation, platform parity and user feedback, so a usage increase alone should not be reported as proof of correct component use or system quality. (low confidence)
UXPin recommends explicit approval rights for components, variants, breaking changes and exceptions, plus a logged exception path with an expiry date or migration plan. (low confidence)

UXPin describes a component lifecycle from proposal through review, build, documentation, release, adoption measurement and deprecation; it asks for use-case and reuse evidence before adding variants. (low confidence)

In Curtis’s spec-driven approach, component specifications describe the public API, variant rules and composed examples; supplemental requirements capture behavior, accessibility and state precedence such as `disabled` over `read-only`. (low confidence)

Communicate component retirement before removal: GOV.UK describes deprecation as advance notice of a future breaking change, while zeroheight warns that deleting an in-use component immediately can leave gaps and lost references. (medium confidence)

zeroheight recommends inspecting component dependencies and replacement fit before retirement: check direct template usage, nesting in larger components, whether replacements differ by use case, and whether contained components also become redundant. (low confidence)

Preply explicitly avoids mandatory visual-coverage targets: bespoke needs and third-party components can justify lower coverage. Its account also warns that popular public pages can obscure other teams in aggregate measurements. (low confidence)

GOV.UK Frontend v5 guidance uses patch increments for bug fixes, minor increments for new features and major increments for potentially required consumer changes; it still directs consumers to read release notes and test upgrades because breaking impact depends on usage. (low confidence)

GOV.UK publication criteria require evidence from a representative sample including users with disabilities; limited deployment is acceptable when tested contexts are stated and wider feedback is encouraged. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)

Matan Rosen recommends component specifications that enumerate states and variants, anatomy, boundaries, empty and error states, text constraints and keyboard interactions. This makes behavior and limits explicit alongside appearance. (low confidence)

Capozzi’s migration account identifies a coordination failure mode: automatic replacement leaves special cases that require consuming teams’ knowledge and roadmap capacity. Its numerical automation estimates are the author’s guesses, so they should not become general migration benchmarks. (low confidence)

Société Générale’s practitioner account describes a council that checks consistency, reviews documentation and supports contributions. Council membership depends on available time and enthusiasm; this is a contextual operating model rather than evidence that one structure fits every organization. (low confidence)

Nathan Curtis argues that federation should augment dedicated central capacity rather than replace it. His practitioner account describes a stalled system after the responsible team was disbanded without relieving federated contributors of their existing responsibilities; it is not a controlled comparison of governance models. (low confidence)

Deprecation should include a transition plan and visibility into consumption rather than immediate deletion. Zeroheight recommends communication and usage analysis; Mae Capozzi describes replacement parity, preventing new deprecated uses, automation and product-team help for cases requiring manual migration. (medium confidence)

Preply describes visual coverage as a measure of design-system usage in rendered products, complementing static code analysis. Its account says coverage is one metric among several and is a diagnostic signal rather than a score teams must maximize. (low confidence)
Preply distinguishes codebase usage from what users actually encounter; its visual coverage measures use of design-system components in products, rather than proving correct usage. (low confidence)

UXPin presents governance structure as a tradeoff: a small or overloaded central team can bottleneck contributions, while federated contributions require communication and coordination and may introduce inconsistency when guidelines are not followed. (low confidence)

Contribution governance can separate proposal eligibility from publication readiness: GOV.UK checks usefulness and uniqueness before reviewing usability, consistency and versatility; Société Générale describes a single request entry point with council triage and explicit outcomes. (medium confidence)

GOV.UK Frontend v5 documents deprecation as advance notice of a future breaking change, usually in the next major version. Addressing deprecations incrementally reduces the work needed for a later major upgrade. (low confidence)

GOV.UK’s August 2026 research on prototype lifecycle labels found that “Trial” was broadly understood, while “Needs review” created uncertainty about onward use. Participants wanted context about accessibility testing and future changes. The findings support explaining what each label means and what action users should take; they do not establish that these proposed labels were deployed. (low confidence)

GOV.UK contribution guidance separates proposal review for usefulness and uniqueness from implementation review for usability, consistency and versatility. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08)
